title: Insight
hook: seeing impermanence, unsatisfactoriness and not-self in your own experience

segments.voice: Yesterday: samatha, calm, and your line, two wings. Did ten slow breaths let the snow settle before a decision? Day two hundred ninety-six, and the other wing.

You've probably seen a sign for it. A ten-day silent retreat. No phones, no talking, no eye contact, up before dawn, meditating most of the day. People come back from those courses and struggle to describe what happened. Some say it was the hardest thing they've ever done. Some say it changed how they see everything. The courses have spread from Myanmar and India to nearly every country on earth, and most run on donations. The word on the sign is the same everywhere. It's the second wing of yesterday's bird. Today: insight.
screen: `A TEN-DAY SILENT RETREAT.` → `THE HARDEST THING, OR EVERYTHING CHANGED.` → `THE SECOND WING.`

segments.voice: Vipassanā. Passanā means seeing. Vi can mean clearly, or in different ways, or through. Seeing clearly. Seeing through. What does insight see? The Theravada tradition says: three marks that belong to everything that's put together. Anicca: it changes. Dukkha: because it changes, it can't finally satisfy. Anattā: there's no fixed self inside it that owns it. You've heard these before on this path. Insight is the difference between hearing them and seeing them in your own experience. The Dhammapada puts the first mark this way, in Max Müller's English: "'All created things perish,' he who knows and sees this becomes passive in pain; this is the way to purity." Passive in pain is Müller's old phrasing for growing weary of what causes suffering, letting go. The next two verses say the same about the other marks. Notice the verb: knows and sees. Not believes. Insight practice turns the attention on the moment-to-moment stream of body and mind: an itch that arises, peaks and fades; a thought that seems solid, then dissolves; a mood you'd sworn was you, gone by lunch. Seen over and over, the tradition says, the grip loosens by itself. In the last century and a half, Burmese teachers brought this practice out of the monasteries and taught it to lay people. The monk Ledi Sayadaw was one of the first. A layman, U Ba Khin, taught S. N. Goenka, who took ten-day courses to the world. Tomorrow, another Burmese method. Today, one instruction. Don't take my word for it. See clearly.
screen: `VI + PASSANĀ: SEEING THROUGH.` · `THREE MARKS.` · `KNOWS AND SEES, NOT BELIEVES.` · `FROM MONASTERY TO LAY PEOPLE.` · then, large: `SEE CLEARLY.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the breath settle for a few moments. Then begin to watch change. Pick any sensation, the touch of your hands, the air at the nose, a small ache, and watch it closely. Does it stay exactly the same? Notice it shift, pulse, fade, return. When a sound comes, notice it begin and end. When a thought comes, notice it arrive and leave. Nothing to fix. Just see each thing change. The bell holds the time.
Vipassana. Insight: seeing change, unsatisfactoriness and not-self in your own experience, not just believing them.
Your line: see clearly. Today, when a strong mood arrives, watch it the way you'd watch weather: when it came, how it changes, when it goes. Day two hundred ninety-six.

howItsDone: Vipassana is taught in Theravada monasteries and in lay meditation centers worldwide, often in silent retreats of ten days or more; S. N. Goenka's courses and the Mahasi centers are two of the best known.

fork.setup: during a sit, an itch appears on your nose. you're practicing insight. what do you do?
options: watch it arise, peak and change, and see what happens.
decide it means you're doing it wrong.
fork.reveal: insight practice turns attention to how each sensation changes; seen closely, even an itch shows the first mark.

original.note: Pali vipassanā: insight, clear seeing; Sanskrit vipaśyanā.

trapdoor: what you thought: vipassana is a relaxation technique.
what it means: seeing change, unsatisfactoriness and not-self directly, until the grip loosens.
what a scholar hears: the modern lay vipassana movement began in colonial Burma with Ledi Sayadaw, partly to protect the teaching when the monarchy fell.

sources.work: The Dhammapada (Sacred Books of the East, vol. 10)

notes: Check Müller's exact wording of Dhammapada 277 in SBE 10 (quoted from memory).
The gloss of 'passive in pain' (Pali nibbindati dukkhe, grows disenchanted with suffering) is the writer's; confirm.
'Don't take my word for it' is spoken in the narrator's voice as the manuscript allows, echoing the Kalama Sutta's spirit; Keeper may prefer 'the tradition says: see for yourself'.
Ledi Sayadaw (1846–1923), U Ba Khin (1899–1971), S. N. Goenka (1924–2013): confirm.
Trapdoor claim about motivations after the fall of the Burmese monarchy (1885) follows Erik Braun, The Birth of Insight (2013): confirm.
